items.titleEn: Gabriel enjoying his football after positive start
items.summaryEn: Big Gabi discussed beating Chelsea, facing Sunderland and different defensive partners
bodyEn: Gabriel has enjoyed our start to the 2026/27 season, playing every minute as we've made it five wins from five in all competitions, conceding just one goal along the way.

Our Brazilian defender played 49 games last season as we won the Premier League title and reached both the Champions League and Carabao Cup finals. After an impressive campaign last time around, Big Gabi feels we can do even better this season.
"We want more," Gabi said, "we want to win as many major trophies as possible.
"I think we have to have that pressure on us because we want it.
"The way we believe in each other and the way we communicate on the pitch and off the pitch makes it a real pleasure to be here every single day with them."
Our biggest test of the new season so far came last weekend when we battled to a 2-1 win over Chelsea at Emirates Stadium.
Big Gabi was especially proud of our response to going behind early on, before he came back to maintain our 100% start.
"It felt very good. The way we played was unbelievable. Everyone on the pitch, the way we ran, we're very happy.
"We know Chelsea's qualities as well, so I think the way we came back in the game was unbelievable."
One of the challenges for Big Gabi at the start of this season has been the range of defensive partners, with William Saliba our injured.
But Gabi feels just as comfortable with Cristhian Mosquera or new signing Ezri Konsa alongside him as he does with Wilo.
"It doesn't matter who is playing at the back," Gabi said, "we talk a lot every day.
"The best thing is to be connected to each other, communicate a lot.
"We have amazing players at this club. I think the squad is very strong, so I'm very happy. I'm happy to have [Ezri] Konsa here with us, he's a big player, a strong player."
As well as partnering with Ezri, our Brazilian has a new national teammate to play with at club level after Bruno Guimaraes joined us from Newcastle.
Gabi admitted that he'd spoken to Bruno about the move during this summer's World Cup, and is delighted to have his friend in north London.
"I'm very happy to have him here. We were at the World Cup together and I told him to come to Arsenal!
"We are very close , I hope we enjoys every day. He's a very good player, he's going to enjoy this club a lot."
After beating Napoli 1-0 on Wednesday night, our next test sees us take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.
After drawing 2-2 with the Black Cats last November, Gabi knows we're in for a difficult assignment on Saturday night.
"We know with the experience from last year, we know it's a tough place to go, but we must earn the right to go there and get the three points."

bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.

Arsenal’s flight to Italy for their Champions League opener against Napoli this week was delayed for more than five hours, with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time. The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe, thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner.

Arteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previously employed pickpockets during pre-season training camps and preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker. The Arsenal manager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else. Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.

“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘OK, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”

Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”

Arsenal travel to Sunderland on Saturday night looking to extend their 100% start to the new campaign after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last year. Leandro Trossard scored Arsenal’s second goal before Brian Brobbey’s late equaliser and Arteta contrasted the Belgium forward’s reaction to leaving in the summer with that of Gabriel Jesus. “No one told me nothing,” said the Brazilian, who was made to train separately from the rest of Arsenal’s squad before moving to Barcelona. Trossard, meanwhile, was at the Emirates for last week’s win over Chelsea having joined Beskitas in July.

“Very surprised, to be fair, especially because with Gabriel I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” said Arteta. “And the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don’t know. It’s OK. Sometimes I understand when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don’t expect. Those things are reactive. Somebody has to be the bad cop; if I have to be, I have to be.

“What is important is normally what happens three months later, six months later. When Trossard comes in, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relation you have with all the players that they left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that’s the same case.”

items.titleEn: FPL Focus: Who should you consider for Gameweek 4?
items.summaryEn: All the best tips from the FPL for gameweek four as we take on Sunderland
bodyEn: We're three wins from three in the 2026/27 Premier League season as we get ready to face Sunderland in a pulsating weekend of action. For the millions of Fantasy Premier League managers, the opening three weekends will have left them delighted with their early squad choice, or already pondering their first wildcard at this early stage.
Regardless of your situation, we're here to give you a helping hand for your line-ups to get the best results in Gameweek 4.
BEST OF ARSENAL

Martin Odegaard (£6.7m) was the star of the show in our 2-1 win against Chelsea in Gameweek 3. Our captain notched his second double-digit haul of the season returning a goal and maximum bonus points. Odegaard racked up four chances created, two shots and registered a match-high expected goal involvement (xGI) tally of 1.60. The Norwegian has scored more Fantasy points than any other Arsenal player (24), thanks to two goals and six bonus points.

Making his first start in a Gunners shirt, Ezri Konsa (£4.4m) led the way for defensive contributions and reached the required threshold for the two additional points. Despite not keeping a clean sheet, Konsa finished the match on a score of four. Over 350,000 managers have transferred-in the England international to make him the most-bought defender of the Gameweek so far.

Elsewhere, Christos Tzolis (£6.4m) bounced back from his half-time substitution in Gameweek 2 by notching his second assist for the season and playing the full 90 minutes. The Greek international continues to look like great value for money in Fantasy. Riccardo Calafiori (£5.8m) showed why he is the most-selected defender in the game, despite blanking, by racking up 0.39 expected goals and having two shots on goal. The Italian has risen in price for the third time this season and was rested in the Champions League midweek.
TOP TRANSFERS IN

Outside of Arsenal, Morgan Rogers (£7.6m) is one of the most transferred-in players ahead of Gameweek 4, being bought by over half a million managers and rising in price. The Englishman who is yet to blank in Fantasy this season, picking up two assists and a goal, set-up four goals in the League Cup on Wednesday. Cole Palmer (£9.7m) is another Chelsea player being bought ahead of the Blues’ home fixture against newly-promoted Hull City.

Maxim De Cuyper (£4.8m) continues to be well-bought after picking up an assist against Leeds United. The Belgium left-back continues to play out-of-position on the left wing for Brighton. In Gameweek 1, the Seagull notched a goal and assist to return a massive 17-point haul. De Cuyper faces Coventry in Gameweek 4, who are yet to pick up a point so far this season.

Liverpool duo Cody Gakpo (£7.2m) and Alexander Isak (£9.1m) are also popular acquisitions for the Reds’ home clash against Fulham. The duo currently boast over one million combined transfers ahead of deadline. Opponents Fulham have conceded the most big chances of any team this season and have shipped seven goals so far. A word of warning on Gakpo though, he is currently yellow flagged in the game after missing out in midweek due to a knock.
GAMEWEEK 4 TIPS
Make sure you don’t miss the deadline! Finalise your team by 1.30pm BST on Saturday, September 12 ahead of the 3pm matches.

Plenty of managers will be activating chips this week, with the Wildcard set to be the most popular. Deciding between triple Arsenal defence or selecting a Gunners attacker like Odegaard or Bukayo Saka (£9.5m) looks to be one of the key decisions for those playing this chip.

Elsewhere, the Free Hit is a strong option to load-up on Chelsea and Liverpool players for their favourable home matches; while Cole Palmer is drawing the attention of those with the Triple Captain left.

items.titleEn: Arteta on learning lessons for Sunderland trip
items.summaryEn: Mikel assesses our trip to Sunderland and being adaptable in a crisis
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta cannot wait to face Sunderland and is confident his side has learned a lot of lessons from last season's trip to the Stadium of Light.
After falling a goal behind, we fought back through Bukayo Saka and Leandro Trossard, only to be pegged back by a late Brian Brobbey equaliser.

Reflecting on the result last November, Mikel said: "We experienced last season how tough it’s going to be tomorrow night. It’s an unbelievable atmosphere, and it’s great to play in these kinds of games.

"We know how ready they’re going to be, we have prepared the game, we’re going to finalise the game today. We know the importance of it and we’ll be ready tomorrow to be on that pitch. We’ll compete like we always do, we’ll try to be better than the opponent and win the game.

"Last year, we dropped points there, especially in the last minutes. We experienced and learned a lot from that game. Tomorrow, again, we'll discuss many things that we need to be aware of and where we want to take the game, what their qualities are and how we’ll try to nullify them.

"[There are] plenty of things to improve, to be alert to, and some others that we have to continue to do because we did some great things that night and other things that we will discuss to prepare for the game."
Recovering in adversity is a sign of champions, and something Mikel is keen to get out of his players in any scenario.
The side faced travel delays before our match against Napoli, but Mikel knows these are the sort of obstacles his side needs to be the best.

"I love those challenges," he said. "I try to create them in pre-season. So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, [if you] get to the stadium very late, change the routine and suddenly the players have to do something else.

"Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there's so much traffic. So when that happens, adapt to it. Okay, we have another two or three hours on the plane. How can we use them: play together, spend some time together, sleep? Use it, but certainly don't complain and then use it as an excuse because that's not helpful at all."

items.titleEn: Arteta's update on White, Mosquera and Timber
items.summaryEn: The boss provided the latest on our defensive trio
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has provided an update on the fitness of Ben White, Jurrien Timber and Cristhian Mosquera ahead of our trip to the Stadium of Light to face Sunderland on Saturday.

While Cristhian and Jurrien are looking to work their way back into the side after respective spells on the sidelines, Ben was seen limping towards the end of our 1-0 win over Napoli on Wednesday night.
But the boss confirmed the England defender is "fine" and will be in contention to feature in Saturday's game.
Cristhian and Timber meanwhile are nearing returns having missed out on our first Champions League game of the season.
"[Cristhian's] doing really well," the boss said at the Sobha Realty Training Centre on Friday, "let's see if he can get [back] for this game or the next one.
"[With Jurrien], let's see. We have another training session. He's been doing really well, he's been training with us now for a few days, and he looks in good shape."
While we await the return of some of our defenders, we've enjoyed a full compliment of attacking players in the early stages of the season.

New signing Christos Tzolis has hit the ground running in north London, and Mikel feels that the combinations he's forming with other members of our squad, such as the link up he's established with Martin Odegaard, will benefit us as the season goes on.
"Hopefully those relationships are great between all the players," the boss said, "that's what we try to develop.
"There is certainly a start there, and let's see where we have a bigger example, how this develops, but it's a really good sign."

items.titleEn: Every word from Arteta's pre-Sunderland presser
items.summaryEn: Read everything Mikel Arteta had to say to the media before our trip to the Stadium of Light
bodyEn: Fresh from our victory in Naples, Mikel Arteta has been speaking with the press before we take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.
The boss gave a team news update, reflected on our draw at Sunderland last season and much more during the press conference at the Sobha Realty Training Centre.
Read a full transcript below, with a video of the press conference to follow!
on team news after Napoli:No, all good.
on White:He’s fine.
on Mosquera:He’s doing really well. Let’s see if he can get [back] for this game or the next one, it will be around that time.
on Timber:Let’s see, we have another training session. He’s been doing really well, he’s been training with us now for a few days and he looks in good shape.

on our Ballon d’Or nominations:It says about where the club is at the moment, how well the club is doing. I think obviously the consistency that we’ve shown in our performances. Then those individual rewards are because the team does an incredible job together, so it’s good to see, they have transformed that into major trophies, that’s the important thing.
on if he will win the head coach category:That’s not up to me, but it’s a privilege to be there for sure.
on if Rice should win:I don’t get to vote, so I’ll leave that to the specialists.

on the potential to have seven Arsenal players in the England squad:Let’s see what Thomas [Tuchel] decides first and after that we can talk about it. I’m really happy with our players, the variety that we have within the squad, the balance within the squad, especially the personalities and the different qualities that we have managed to put together.

on the importance of the English contingent to our side:Very important, not only within the squad but also within the staff, within the club and to make sure that this culture and the roots are very clear and that they are very attached to our identity and our values.

on the understanding between Odegaard and Tzolis:Hopefully those relationships are great between all the players, that’s what we try to develop. There is certainly a start there and let’s see when we have a bigger example, how this develops, but it’s a really good sign.

on the gap between ourselves and Man City’s probability of winning the Premier League:I’m only interested in the probability of winning tomorrow - that’s the most important thing. To make that as high as possible, and in order to achieve that, you really need to earn it on the pitch against a really tough opponent, as we know.
on a 0.05% chance of relegation:Always on your toes.

on how to coach Odegaard’s game IQ or if the onus is more on him:Both - obviously the attention you put in around the team, the roles, clarity, concepts and principles you have to apply to be efficient, because you can be there. If the timing is not good, the momentum and the shift in position or the rotation is not good, there is no efficiency. That’s what we try to create with the players.

on how Rice on the right and Lewis-Skelly coming in from the left helps our attack:It depends on our players, and depends for sure on the behaviour of the opponent, the kind of attitude they have, especially in different phases of play. In relation to that, it’s to try and have the quality of our players to be as vertical and progressive as possible, and to put the players in the best possible scenarios as often as we can.

on what qualities we look for in our players when things are going well:The next day - for example, how they do their recovery, how they interact with each other and their energy, the way they train the next morning, the attention they’re paying in meetings, their attention span when you look at each other in their eyes, and how much they are talking about the next game or what they have to learn from the previous game. It’s a lot to observe.

on Havertz’s best position:The best position is in relation to what the game demands and what the team demands on the day - to be as efficient and unpredictable as possible. Kai is extremely intelligent - that’s his biggest quality. He understands the game - he’s five, 10 seconds ahead. He knows what’s happening, he doesn’t need to think about it - he just acts, and it makes the people around him better which is another massive quality. On top of that, he’s scoring goals, producing chances. He’s outstanding, and he’s in a great emotional state at the moment.

on if his best position can change game by game:It can, yes, because you can play as a nine, but what do you play as a nine? What’s your role with and without the ball? It’s a lot of things, a position on the pitch. When you put it in a tactical world, you probably put the nine in the centre - but then what do you do when there’s a set-piece, a transition moment, a high press, what if the goalkeeper is right or left-footed? There are a lot of factors that are going to take that space and the initial position to a different dimension.

on being the team that everyone has to catch:We have to focus on the next match. We experienced last season how tough it’s going to be tomorrow night. It’s an unbelievable atmosphere, and it’s great to play in these kinds of games. We know how ready they’re going to be, we have prepared the game, we’re going to finalise the game today. We know the importance of it and we’ll be ready tomorrow to be on that pitch. We’ll compete like we always do, we’ll try to be better than the opponent and win the game.

on our previous record against Sunderland:Last year, we dropped points there, especially in the last minutes. We experienced and learned a lot from that game. Tomorrow, again, we'll discuss many things that we need to be aware of and where we want to take the game, what their qualities are and how we’ll try to nullify them.

on when pre-match routines are shaken up, such as flight delays:I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season. So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So get to the stadium very late, change the routine and suddenly the players have to do something else. Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there's so much traffic and I don't want the players, but not only the players, the staff as well, panicking. So when that happens, adapt to it. Okay, we have another two or three hours on the plane. How can we use them, play together, spend some time together, sleep? Use it, but certainly don't complain and then use it as an excuse because that's not helpful at all.

on comments from Martinelli and Jesus:Very surprised, to be fair. Especially because with Gabi, I had an individual talk in the dressing room. I don't know what words were said, it's fine, and the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don't know, it's okay. Sometimes I understand that when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don't expect, those things are reactive. Somebody has to be there to back up. If I have to be, I have to be and I understand. What's important is normally what happens three months later, six months later, when Trossard comes in, he's in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relationship you have, and thanks God so far, with all the players that left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that's the same case.

on if Konsa has surprised us with how quickly he’s settled:Well, it's certainly something to admire because it's not easy at all and you should not take it for granted. But after talking to a lot of people that have worked with him, whether they're staff members or players, I already had a sense of the way everybody was talking about him, that he's a person that is great at gathering people together, he has a real personality, a lot of leadership skills, and you saw the first day he just trained the way he was talking, the way he was presenting himself. It was very impressive and so far he's done a really good job.

on if his performances make us relaxed with Saliba’s recovery:Relaxed obviously. We had him out and Jurrien [Timber] out for long periods, and then we had the issue with Mosquera, so we were really, really thin at the back. So we needed to put another good player in that position, especially with the expectation that we have the amount of minutes that they are going to have to try to play. We've done it and so far it's working well.

on if he’d have liked to have been able to rotate White and Timber a lot more:That was one of the challenges last year, especially when we have two or three injuries within the same line, sometimes in the same position as well. So hopefully this season we have a bit more luck and we can manage that better, and if we manage that better, probably the likelihood of them getting injuries is going to be low.

on if their injuries are down to the demands of the position or just bad luck:With Jurrien in the last three seasons as well, he had the ACL, it was a long-term injury that has consequences afterwards, and then Ben [White] was out and you start to load a player for five weeks and our schedule begins to play 15 games in that period. I mean, the probability of something happening, it is bigger, and yeah, the full-backs' position nowadays, they do have some huge physical demands.

on how big the role of competition he faced at Barcelona has played in building our squad:A huge one. At that point, I used different terminology. It was a great level of competition, the best I have experienced in my career, obviously, certainly at that age. But then there was a really great sense of supporting and helping your teammates as well, and that balance, I think, between us, we cannot just compete. I think we need to cooperate and we need to understand each other's role and we need to be happy for the teammates' success, and that's what we try to do always.

on if there’s anything from last season’s trip to Sunderland that we can bring into this weekend:Plenty of things. Plenty of things to improve, to be alert to, and some others that we have to continue to do because we did some great things that night and other things that we will discuss to prepare for the game.

items.summaryEn: Our Premier League 2 campaign continues with a London derby against the Blues
bodyEn: Our under-21s take on Chelsea in a Premier League 2 London derby on Saturday afternoon at Mangata Developments Stadium (2pm UK).
A solid start to the season has seen us take draws from each of our first two games against defending champions Brighton and last season's play-off quarter-finalists Crystal Palace.

As well as our positive start in PL2, several of our under-21s squad were involved in our 2-1 win over Napoli in our UEFA Youth League opener on Wednesday afternoon, a game which saw Luis Munoz strike a stoppage-time winner.
THE OPPOSITION

While Chelsea's under-21s reached the play-off quarter-finals themselves last time around, the Blues' under-18s side won the U18s Premier League, with some players from that side since moving up to the PL2 set-up.
After a surprise defeat to Bournemouth in their opening game, Chelsea battled to a 2-2 draw with Bristol Rovers before beating the League Two side on penalties in their opening EFL Trophy game.

The young Blues then registered their first league win of the season in sensational style, scoring in the 89th and 92nd minutes to beat West Ham 5-4 in what was comfortably the game of the PL2 season so far.
HOW TO FOLLOW

As with all Premier League 2 fixtures, entry to Saturday's game at Mangata Developments Stadium is free, and with our first team clash at Sunderland not getting underway until 8pm, get down to the ground for your Saturday afternoon helping of football.

For those who can't make it to the ground, live updates will be available on our Academy's X account, with a full match report, highlights and interviews with head coach David Horseman and one of our young Gunners available after the game.

items.titleEn: U18s preview: Arsenal v Crystal Palace
items.summaryEn: Our young Gunners take on the Eagles in north London on Saturday
bodyEn: Our under-18s face Crystal Palace at the Sobha Realty Training Centre on Saturday morning (11am UK) looking to continue our positive form.
We got our UEFA Youth League campaign underway with a late 2-1 win over Napoli on Wednesday, with several under-18s players involved in the success.
Before our win in Italy, our young Gunners registered their first league win of the season, beating Southampton 1-0 through Maalik Hashi's early strike.
THE OPPOSITION

Having started the season with a win, the Eagles have struggled in recent weeks. Their 3-1 win over West Ham United gave them three points right off the bat, but they are yet to add to that tally since the opening day.
Palace have conceded nine goals in their last three league games, losing heavily to Southampton and Tottenham either side of a 1-0 defeat to 2025 U18s champions Aston Villa.
The south London side also got off to a difficult start in the Premier League Cup, losing 2-1 away to Nottingham Forest.
HOW TO FOLLOW
Supporters can stay up to date with the action from the Sobha Realty Training Centre by following live updates on our Academy X channel.

Post-match, a full match report will be available on The Arsenal app and on Arsenal.com, with highlights from the game and interviews with a coach and one of our young Gunners available the following day.

bodyEn: With 10 top-flight goal contributions between them across three games already this season, the Chelsea trio of Morgan Rogers, João Pedro and Cole Palmer are the early pace-setters for the Premier League’s most prolific, fluid and high-octane attacking unit. But on the occasion of his 100th Premier League appearance, a scruffier and more ungainly unit will be hoping to steal their thunder, as high-flying Hull try to register a top-flight win against Chelsea for the very first time. Yet to score this season but with a couple of near misses to his name, what Oli McBurnie has thus far lacked in goal contributions he has more than made up for with selfless graft and off-the-ball grunt work, making a total mockery of Steve Clarke’s decision not to include him in Scotland’s World Cup squad. The Hull striker ought to prove a real handful for a decidedly porous home defence, and a goal would be a fitting way to mark a century of Premier League appearances. Chelsea have not won any of their past four league matches against promoted opposition and, given Hull’s blistering start to the season, victory on Saturday seems anything but a foregone conclusion. Barry Glendenning
Chelsea v Hull, Saturday 3pm (all times BST)

This might be an opportune moment for Álvaro Arbeloa to meet Andoni Iraola, though perhaps not his Liverpool team. With three defeats and seven goals conceded from his first three Premier League games as Fulham head coach, questions are already being asked over the former Liverpool defender’s ambitious approach. Just as they were when Iraola failed to win any of his first nine league games in charge of Bournemouth. Trust yourself and the process, might be the Liverpool head coach’s advice if asked. Fulham have been creative under Arbeloa but are easily exposed defensively. Liverpool, starting to click in attack under their new head coach, have the assets to exploit Fulham’s weaknesses and subject Arbeloa to an uncomfortable Anfield return. Iraola’s wide options could be reduced, however, with Bradley Barcola suffering cramp on Wednesday – his first start since France’s World Cup semi-final loss – and Cody Gakpo nursing a minor injury. Andy Hunter
Liverpool v Fulham, Saturday 3pm

Cheick Doucouré has had a rotten run of luck with injuries. Just when the Mali midfielder looked as if he was ready to make a first Crystal Palace appearance since January 2025 in Tuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Middlesbrough, he was taken ill. Pierre Sage revealed last week that Doucouré looked as if he had “given him one million dollars” when he was informed he would be part of the matchday squad at Fulham, where Palace got off the mark with a 3-2 victory. Sage has confirmed that the 26-year-old, who has been sidelined with two serious knee injuries but was once a transfer target for Liverpool, could be involved against Ipswich at Selhurst Park on Saturday. Whenever he does return it is sure to be a heartwarming moment. Ed Aarons
Crystal Palace v Ipswich, Saturday 3pm

The midfield battle between Brentford and Bournemouth will be crucial on Saturday, with Vitaly Janelt and Mamadou Sangaré setting the tempo for Keith Andrews’ physical side. Brentford top the Premier League for aerial duels won (22.3 per 90 mins), interceptions (11.3 per 90), and fouls committed (16.3 per 90). “They defend well as a team, their high pressing is good,” said Bournemouth’s Marco Rose, who is hoping to guide his side to a first Premier League victory of the season. “Their transition, they have fast players. They have quality everywhere on the pitch, and every situation.” Rose’s answer for Brentford’s aggressiveness should be Alex Scott, who leads his team for interceptions and has drawn nine fouls so far this campaign – the fourth-highest tally in the league. Late drama could also be the deciding factor at the Vitality Stadium. Despite leading in all three of their opening league fixtures, Bournemouth have picked up just two points and four of their five goals conceded have arrived from the 84th minute onwards. History favours their opponents too, as the Cherries have failed to win any of their eight top-flight meetings with the Bees. Yara El-Shaboury
Bournemouth v Brentford, Saturday 3pm

A summer of change at Aston Villa inevitably prompted plenty of noise but most of their new signings were long-standing targets, none more so than Nicolas Jackson. Unai Emery kickstarted Jackson’s career at Villarreal and, after reuniting at Villa, the Senegal striker scored his first goal at Club Brugge on Tuesday after his initial £47.5m move. Jackson has replaced Ollie Watkins, who proved a reliable source of goals across six straight top-flight seasons, and the early evidence has been encouraging. “I had a couple of fights with him when he was at Chelsea so when he first came in I thought: ‘What’s he going to be like?’ but he’s a brilliant guy,” said the Villa captain, John McGinn. “There’s a lot of expectation with the transfer fee but he’s going to be a huge player for us.” Ben Fisher
Aston Villa v Nottingham Forest, Saturday 3pm

Only the most pessimistic home fans at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium will be gripped by anything resembling the kind of dread, anxiety and outright terror that accompanied Everton’s visit on the final day of last season, but the return of David Moyes’ side so early in the current campaign will still make for nervous viewing. With no goals and just one point on the board after three league games, fan faith in Roberto De Zerbi – and the hundreds of millions of pounds lavished upon new signings – has created a prevailing presumption that Tottenham will soon start firing on at least some, if not all, cylinders. In Everton, Spurs welcome a team whose record in this corner of north London is worse than any other top-flight side’s. Should they fail to beat a team who have taken just seven points from the past 51 available to them away at Tottenham, the sounds of early but outright mutiny are likely to be audible from the stands. BG
Tottenham v Everton, Saturday 5.30pm

Old acquaintance will be renewed at the Stadium of Light on Saturday evening. While Sunderland’s captain and midfield anchor, Granit Xhaka, needs no introduction to his former north London public, the home centre-half Dan Ballard is a former Arsenal youth captain who joined the Gunners’ academy at the age of eight. Then there is Bruno Guimarães. Newcastle’s former captain can expect a hot reception as his new side aim to extend their season-opening run of five straight wins (including the Community Shield). “Arsenal are flying, they’re one of the best teams in Europe,” says Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s manager. “It will be challenging but I’m very excited to experience this situation again.” Thanks to goals from Ballard and Brian Brobbey, Le Bris choreographed a 2-2 Premier League draw against Mikel Arteta’s side on Wearside last November. “When you face a strong opponent you can become a bit shy but the most important thing is to be ourselves,” says Le Bris. “Arsenal are so adaptive they will find solutions, so we must be flexible.” Louise Taylor
Sunderland v Arsenal, Saturday 8pm

One of three teams, along with Aston Villa and Tottenham, yet to score a top-flight goal this season, Coventry were extremely unfortunate not to break their duck at Manchester City last weekend. Their having narrowly avoided handing Frank Lampard’s side an early opener, it took a string of excellent saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma to ensure City took three points at the death. “They played really well against Manchester City and created a lot of chances,” said Fabian Hürzeler, who takes his Brighton team to the CBS Arena on Sunday afternoon. Having been scathing in his criticism of his own side’s lack of energy and intensity in their woeful first-half performance against Leeds, the German will be aware that a similarly lethargic performance from his team is unlikely to go unpunished. Particularly away from home against a promoted team that may be firing blanks, but visibly grew in confidence with each passing minute of their defeat by one of the league’s best teams. BG
Coventry v Brighton, Sunday 2pm

Manchester derby No 199 features a fascinating showdown between two young managers operating in the sport’s rarefied air: Michael Carrick, 45, who seeks to guide Manchester United to an 82nd victory in the fixture, and Enzo Maresca, 46, who aims for Manchester City’s 63rd. As the great Pep Guardiola’s successor, the visiting Italian can be delighted at his team’s perfect record from their four games under him since the Community Shield defeat. Carrick, though, should be disappointed at the return from an opening three matches as United’s permanent manager: a defeat at Hull and draw at Everton, with the 5-2 home win over Ipswich sandwiched between. United fans will protest beforehand about the club’s approach to eradicating ticket touting, and the occasion should be particularly spicy and vibrant. Jamie Jackson
Manchester United v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm

Two teams unbeaten in the Premier League this season, two German managers in the dugouts and a Monday night goalkeeping beauty contest at Elland Road. While Daniel Farke welcomes his compatriot Matthias Jaissle to West Yorkshire for the first time, James Trafford – the £40m England keeper Newcastle tried to sign on three separate occasions – will be in goal for Leeds. The visitors eventually turned their attentions to the £26m Czechia goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who arrived on Tyneside from Braga in July. So far at least, Jaissle is delighted by the 24-year-old’s performances. “Lukas is an amazing signing,” said Jaissle. “Coming to the Premier League and dealing with the pressure is not easy and, as a keeper, that pressure is something else. I like Lukas a lot. He’s so calm but so mature as well. There’s not even a hint of nervousness. He gives the whole team confidence. That helps a lot.” LT
Leeds v Newcastle, Monday 8pm

bodyEn: During Covid, when sport was back but behind closed doors, I hosted a number of strange online shows to fill the void of real life. The highlight was chatting to Darren Gough about a lifesize bronze rhinoceros for 45 minutes to 15 small boxes on a Zoom call. I don’t recall who it was for and where the rhinoceros came from – but it might be in his garden.

I ended up doing virtual pre-match corporate Zoom calls for Heineken before Europa League games. It was the wifi version of Club Wembley: a Q&A happening on stage between a generic host and some random ex-pro while you’re trying to chat to your mate and eat an unidentified square of meat with some dauphinoise potatoes.

I’d be in my little square talking to Luis García in his little square about the ghost goal while an assorted group of faces and living rooms or kitchen tables would stare at you, perhaps interested, perhaps not. Did they even want to be there? Were we on mute while someone from marketing was filling a spare box on my laptop watching Death In Paradise on the TV behind me?

Certainly it was hard to create an amazing vibe with Mark van Bommel while his internet connection crashed and a little note on a Google doc appeared telling me to fill for 25 minutes with my favourite memories of the Europa League. Did these disembodied heads in front of me want the deep dive they got on Tony Parks’ heroics in 1984? How many of them knew about Gary Mabbutt playing centre mid and marking Enzo Scifo out of the game?

One of the guests was Dimitar Berbatov. You’d log on half an hour before the show and say hello, try to build some kind of electric rapport with a man in Bulgaria (I think) presumably looking to get in and get out and get back on with whatever social distancing life in Sofia had to offer.

He may have not had Akabusi levels of energy, and his economy of language was not unlike his playing style – why use a hundred words when one will do? But he was into it and did the job perfectly. I absolutely loved Berbatov as a player. Watching him pluck a goalkick out of the sky was more beautiful than watching a lot of other players banging one in from 25 yards. There’s a YouTube video called Dimitar Berbatov – the most underrated first touch ever? It begins with him standing like a lamp-post on the halfway line at Craven Cottage and stopping a crossfield ball stone dead like it’s an anvil.

Back to the Zoom call: I welcome Dimitar, he says hello, I explain my admiration for him, and then say to him that he made football look easy. Did he find it easy? “Yes” he replied. Totally matter of fact. Not trying to impress – just explaining that football was easy.

And for someone like Berbatov, it is a different level to “good touch for a big man”. This is the ultimate type of grace on a football pitch. And perhaps it is reserved for tall, skilful players. I’ve probably used the word languid already but I can’t think of any other use of the word – reserved for players who are almost balletic.

Is it insane to say it’s more aesthetically pleasing than seeing a Messi or a Maradona waltz through a defence? It almost feels as if a low centre of gravity gives you an unfair advantage when it comes to technical skill. No flailing arms and legs to get in the way of you being naturally brilliant.

My biased brain instantly goes to Glenn Hoddle walking through the Oxford United defence with one sway, sitting the keeper down with a movement of the leg. It’s all saying: “This is easier for me than it is for you.”

Which brings us to Kai Havertz – and that dummy against Chelsea. The more and more football becomes that David Mitchell sketch, the more surprised I am that there are still moments in a game that lead to some involuntary noise from deep within.

The ball from Christos Tzolis is definitely for him. Havertz points in front to where he wants the ball. If it’s played there he can probably get a shot away first time. But when it comes, controlling the ball would have been a sensible choice. Back to goal. He could have turned and shot, or just kept the ball. There are lots of good players to pass it to.

Even the way he lifts his left leg at the last second to let the ball run through to Martin Ødegaard is delightful. It’s easy to forget the pace of the game at this level. And when you’re watching on TV where it’s much easier to see the pass you also forget these guys don’t have that view.

Someone somewhere will have done a report on Havertz’s scanning abilities. He doesn’t appear to look behind to check where Ødegaard is. But awareness is hard to calculate. He just knows. And he does it all in a split second, not even. How wonderful that you can do so much without even touching the ball.

A lot of people do quite well out of repeatedly asking whether Arsenal need a centre-forward, so I don’t want to do them out of work. And Havertz isn’t perfect – he isn’t Robbie Fowler in the box. But he has scored in two Champions League finals. He did win the league last season. A lot of beautiful graceful players tend to be beautiful and graceful without delivering on the biggest occasions. Havertz does both. And when he gets it right, it looks easy to him. Imagine finding it easy.

bodyEn: Declan Rice has insisted his body can sustain more than 60 appearances again this season, despite Arsenal’s concerns after he played through pain at the World Cup.

Rice racked up 69 appearances last season for Arsenal and England but revealed during the World Cup he had been managing neural back and hamstring pain, for which he is understood to have received a pain-killing injection, after a hamstring injury in December. It is understood Arsenal are monitoring the 27-year-old’s workload closely after he had only three weeks off before returning to training a week before the Community Shield last month.

Rice came off the bench to replace Bruno Guimarães in the victory over Manchester City in Cardiff and has since started all Arsenal’s matches, with Guimarães’ return from an injury being managed. A major reason why Arsenal bought the Brazil midfielder for £75m from Newcastle was to take some strain off from Rice, although it was noticeable that Rice played all of Wednesday’s Champions League victory at Napoli, with Mikel Merino coming off for Guimarães.

“I think for the last six seasons, even since my West Ham days when they were in Europe, I’ve played 60-plus every season,” Rice said. “So I think it is sustainable because I’ve shown that I can do it.

“It’s just about maintaining it, maintaining the level and the consistency of the performances. For me, that’s the main thing, showing up every week, giving a good account of myself and helping the team win. I’ve been lucky enough to be able to do that. So I’m really hungry to be able to do that again this season.”

It is understood Arsenal offered Rice more time off after the World Cup exploits but that he was keen to return for the start of the season. He is expected to be part of Thomas Tuchel’s squad for Nations League fixtures against Spain, Czechia and Croatia when it is announced next Friday, although whether he features in all four matches remains to be seen, with Arsenal likely to request that he and Bukayo Saka are given another opportunity to rest. Rice said he had found things “tough” during the World Cup but is adamant he is feeling “refreshed”.

“I feel really good at the minute, in really good form, so we’ll make it continue,” he said. “I think everyone knew I had an issue with a neural hamstring. But also on the top of the Premier League season, which was so demanding, the Champions League, to then play a World Cup in that heat really does take its toll. I’m a player that goes on the pitch, wants to be fresh and give 100% every time I put on an England shirt. Yes, there were stages where I felt really, really good and stages where I didn’t feel so good. There were a few things that frustrated me, just with myself, just not feeling 100%. It’s one of those things I just had to manage.”

bodyEn: Valdas Dambrauskas can reel off the questions and answers without a moment’s pause. Who won the first Academy Award for best actor in 1929? It was Emil Jannings, even if someone else might have been tempted to go with Charlie Chaplin. Which country publishes the highest number of daily newspapers? India was the clear winner. Can you name the nation that produces the most electricity per capita in the world? His family, watching back home, clasped heads in hands but he was right: back then, in 2002, the answer was his native Lithuania.

It was enough to win Dambrauskas about £725 in his appearance on Six Zeros – A Million, the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? “At that time it was quite big money,” he says. “I could have bought a flat in my home town; it was a very difficult period there and they were almost free. But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started.”

More than two and a half decades later the story continues at Old Trafford where Dambrauskas will manage the Azerbaijani champions, Sabah, in their Champions League debut on Thursday night. The club’s journey is some tale in itself given Sabah, who came through a dramatic playoff with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, did not exist until 2017. But the path taken by their head coach, a 25-year-old office worker with only a modest football background when his general knowledge skills were put on display, is virtually unparalleled in the modern game.

The money he won helped Dambrauskas and his girlfriend, now wife, to move to north London and establish themselves in an alien environment. “I would have done it anyway – the show came in the middle of our planning,” he says of the move, which became an ambition after a work visit to Norway in 2000.

In Scandinavia he had grasped the extent of the Premier League’s incipient popularity. “I realised this was where real football is. There was no pathway to coaching in Lithuania if you hadn’t been a player; it was impossible. But if I could take a course in England, maybe I could get a chance to step on the ladder at home.”

Dambrauskas spent eight years in London. “The start was very, very difficult. I wasn’t speaking decent English, had no contacts, we didn’t know anyone, we lived in different places, did all kinds of jobs.” He worked in a Muswell Hill pub, delivered newspapers in the area, held down jobs in a nursery school, as a gardener, in sales, and as a self-employed handyman, often simultaneously. The hours were relentless but so was the young man’s focus.

It was a life of an immigrant couple straining every sinew to make their way. Their first child was born in 2004; by then Dambrauskas, who had studied philosophy and social sciences in Lithuania, had enrolled on a sports science and coaching course at London Metropolitan University. From his classroom on the 10th floor he could see the Emirates Stadium sprouting up during that spell of Arsenal invincibility.

The Access to Sports Project, based in Finsbury Park, is a stone’s throw from Arsenal but galaxies away in another sense. It is where Dambrauskas landed his first coaching role, giving sessions to children on Saturday mornings and during school holidays. His next step is all the more remarkable for what has passed since. A round of interviews with Manchester United Soccer Schools brought the chance to work with youngsters around the country, and sometimes on residential trips abroad, under the banner of the then serial title winners. Despite the name it was a far cry from even academy football, but the injection of confidence was transformative.

“It was John Shiels, CEO of the Manchester United Foundation, who gave me the chance. I don’t know what he saw in me – I came in with very broken English and couldn’t express myself as I can now – but he really supported me. At the end of the year he wrote me an appraisal of what I’d done. He said that I was good and could do much more. It was a massive, massive boost for me.”

Through a friend at university, Dambrauskas became involved with the community sports organisation London Tigers. “He told me they always needed coaches.” Eventually he took charge of their semi-professional team, which played in the Spartan South Midlands League. “That was where it really started, coaching at some kind of level.” It meant managing in the FA Vase and the early rounds of the FA Cup.

Dambrauskas also undertook part-time roles at Fulham and Brentford before working as a sports activator for Central YMCA on Tottenham Court Road. He would later take a broader role as sports development manager at London Tigers and took his coaching badges at the London Football Association. “It was a time with no holidays, no days off. I’m a big reader, I read all the time and studied constantly. Sometimes I would finish my university work on the bus. I took every kind of education I could and went to every possible course for every meeting.

“Over the years I had countless interviews for coaching roles, for jobs at centres of excellency in London and outside, so many CVs and applications, but I understood early on that it’s very difficult in England to get on the ladder and that to coach at professional level there was probably impossible. If there is a story where someone is starting in the community scheme and going all the way to become a head coach, I am still to find it.”

By late 2010 he felt ready to pursue what had originally been the end goal: a role in Lithuania. He had started working with their under-17s and agreed to join Ekranas, national champions at the time, as assistant manager. “I had the London Tigers job, 15 hours a week at Brentford and some other things here and there. We had a good life and people thought I was crazy going back home and earning about a fifth of what I was getting in England. But the biggest risk in life is not to take risks.

“I’m forever grateful to my wife for being behind me. We always faced questions: twenty- or thirtysomething guy always studying, trying to work in football, spending all his money on books and courses rather than buying an apartment or something for the family. But I’m very happy with how it turned out and nobody questions those decisions now.”

A kaleidoscopic career bloomed. By December 2014 he had become head coach at Zalgiris Vilnius, the biggest club in Lithuania, winning two more league titles and various cups in a move that felt unthinkable during a humble upbringing in the tiny northern town Pakruojis. “My childhood was not a gift. My dad died when I was 11, and if he knew that I had the job at Zalgiris and that we won so many trophies he would be the happiest person in the world.”

Dambrauskas was not content to stop there. “You are basically nobody and suddenly you get this job. Then you have to prove yourself to everybody again and again and again. So you reached this step on the ladder but what’s next? How do you go to the next level?”

After three years he joined the upwardly mobile Latvian club RFS but harboured concerns about the prospects of leaving the small Baltic football bubble. In the event he need not have worried. Since 2020 he has managed in Croatia with Gorica and Hajduk Split – the latter are “like a tattoo you can’t ever take out, it leaves a mark on you” – in Bulgaria with Ludogorets, in Greece with OFI Crete, in Cyprus with Omonia and with the Hungarian club Diosgyor, who he describes as having “one of the biggest hidden football potentials in Europe”.

Itinerant career paths such as that are, especially in eastern and southern Europe, nothing new. But Sabah had been courting Dambrauskas for two years before he took over in 2025. Once the stars had aligned, he worked a miracle. In 2024-25, Sabah had finished 41 points behind the biggest club in Azerbaijan, Qarabag. Last season Sabah beat them to the title by nine points, earning their crack at the Champions League qualifiers. “I’m really grateful to Qarabag. Every game against them is like taking a master’s degree.”

He waxes lyrical about the stability and facilities available at well-backed Sabah, who were cheered on with fervour befitting a national team when they thrillingly overcame an injury-time deficit against Be’er Sheva. Their success has come with a multinational squad that plays bold, front-foot football in the style he preaches. “But if you don’t understand the human being in front of you, it’s very difficult to pass him your ideas and build trust,” he says.

“What is important in east Africa can be completely different from what someone needs in west Africa or anywhere across Europe. You need to be able to understand different cultures, different traditions, different ways of speaking or behaving. Without that it’s impossible to do anything, and I believe this is where my strength lies.”

It is a glorious piece of circularity that Dambrauskas and Sabah will be watched from the stands on Thursday by a number of his old colleagues from Manchester United Soccer Schools. He beams at the thought; none of this could have seemed remotely attainable during their time on the grass together. “But I had this belief. I had this confidence all the time that I could do it.”

He is equally delighted that the draw has also brought a January visit to Arsenal, that huge presence in his eyeline during those years studying on Holloway Road. He is 49 and would surely lever himself among Europe’s most sought-after coaching properties if he can take Sabah further. “We’re going to respect everyone but not be afraid of anyone. There’s a very nice song by the Lithuanian band Colours of Bubbles called Truth or Dare. Very soon we’re going to find out the truth about ourselves and what we can do. It will be very beneficial for us because I don’t want this club to be a one-day wonder.” As final answers go, it may be his most significant yet.

bodyEn: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.
There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.

“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” the Barcelona head coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”

Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred as Paris Saint-Germain began their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 at the Parc des Princes.

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.

Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.
Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.

Demirovic quickly re-established the lead ​in the ​26th minute and then completed ​the hat-trick with a hooked volley six minutes later. “For me personally it was the perfect start and also for the team as a whole,” Demirovic told Dazn.

West Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.

Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.

The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.

James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. Either Charlton or QPR could have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.

Norwich moved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitors Birmingham 2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.

Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season. Press Association
Sporting, quarter-finalists last season for the first time since 1983, fought back to see off Galatasaray 3-1 in Lisbon.

Galatasaray took an early lead through Gonçalo Inacio’s own goal but Geny ​Catamo punished poor defending to equalise in the 27th minute. Luis Suárez converted a 57th-minute penalty to put Sporting ahead and a blistering free kick from Rodrigo Zalazar six minutes later sealed the win.

items.titleEn: Napoli 0-1 Arsenal: Champions League – as it happened
items.summaryEn: Martin Ødegaard’s goal proved enough for Arsenal to start their campaign with three points2 min: Arsenal are wearing red shorts. Full marks for considering those with colour blindness, and acting with compassion. It doesn’t look good, mind. It’s just not Arsenal.After a moment to remember the victims of the devastating floods in Nepal, Arsenal get the ball rolling. A blistering atmosphere at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona; did anyone expect anything else? Continue reading...
bodyEn: Ed Aarons was in Naples tonight. Here’s his report. Thanks for reading this MBM!

Mikel Arteta – who is unsurprisingly cutting a much more relaxed figure this season – speaks to TNT. “A fully deserved three points … the amount of chances and situations we generated … that doesn’t reflect the result … it should have been a much bigger win … a really tough environment and opponent … the team was superb … attitude … courage … quality … it was a shame we missed so many big chances.”

Post-match postbag. “It’s going to be a tough season for Napoli as their only purchase seems to have been Favasuli from lowly Catanzaro whereas Arsenal have strengthened an already very powerful squad with the likes of Tsolis and Konsa. Essentially, Napoli played for pride and gave a fairly good account of themselves” – Colum Fordham
“Not Viktor’s biggest fan, but the failure of the other players to pass to him this evening - when he’s been in a perfect position to pull the trigger - has been an embarrassment” – Paul G
“I am still irked by the red shorts. Why aren’t Arsenal wearing their third (yellow/blue) kit, as seen at Villa Park? Surely not because of a clash with the officials?” – Aristos Galatopoulos

“Re Saka and rice not being rested: this is an away game at Napoli in the Champions League, with tough games to come. It’s not the Milk Cup against Oxford Utd. You still need to have a real team - points now mean rest is more likely later, when it’s more needed. And that means you simply cannot play both Gyökeres and Madueke. And Rice … well. He plays. Bruno might be a bit annoyed to be a NPC though” – Josh Hardie
There’s a long way to go. So many matches to be played. And it’s a big old table. But here it is anyway.

Arsenal’s performance was more dogged than free-flowing. But they were much the better side, dominating possession and territory, with the lion’s share of the chances. And though some wasteful finishing threatened to spoil all of their hard work, when they finally broke through it was a peach from their captain Martin Odegaard, back to his best. Another assist for Christos Tzolis too. Napoli by contrast have now lost three games on the bounce, their new boss Massimiliano Allegri already under a bit of pressure.
Arsenal start with a deserved victory.
90 min +3: Arsenal have the ball in the net again, Tzolis shooting from an angle on the left, Milinković-Savić spilling into the path of Havertz, who can’t miss. But Havertz was offside.

90 min +2: Now Neres whacks the ball away in frustration, but he’s not booked, the referee having missed it. Gabriel is furious, and runs the risk of picking up a card himself by telling it as he sees it.
90 min +1: Odegaard is booked for lashing a dead ball away, with Napoli preparing to take a quick free kick deep in their own territory.
90 min: There will be four additional minutes.

89 min: Neres pings a cute pass down the inside-left channel, and suddenly De Bruyne is free, on the corner of the six-yard box. De Bruyne has only Raya to beat, but rolls a ball across the face of goal, hoping to find Lucca instead. Lucca’s not there. The crowd groan again, at the latest of De Bruyne’s egregious errors. It’s not been a banner evening for one of the genuine greats of the last decade.
88 min: … Napoli counter, but Neres can’t get on the end of a pass down the middle. Arsenal were light at the back.
87 min: A corner for Arsenal on the right. Madueke wanders in and aims for the top left. The shot is deflected wide left for another corner, from which …
86 min: Lucca is booked for knocking into Gabriel.

85 min: Gilmour is robbed by Zubimendi and sends Guimarães away on the counter. Guimarães slips in Madueke to his right. Madueke is clear! But he can’t slip the ball under Milinković-Savić, who blocks, then spins up and stops Madueke rolling into the empty net. Madueke instead cuts back for Tzolis, whose drive hits the nearest defender. Not sure how Napoli kept that out, but they collectively managed it.
84 min: Favasuli tries to take on Hincapie in a footrace down the right, but the defender’s letting nobody past.
82 min: Guimarães looks for the top-left corner from 25 yards. High and wide. Before Milinković-Savić restarts the game, Zubimendi comes on for White.

80 min: Lucca barrels after a long punt down the middle, but can’t get the ball under control. On the touchline, Massimiliano Allegri, staring down the barrel of a third consecutive defeat so early in his reign, rants and raves in the classic continental style.
78 min: That’s now four assists in five games for Tzolis. Arsenal fans are in great voice, the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona otherwise quiet.
77 min: Napoli respond with a double change, replacing Hojlund and Lobotka with Neres and Lucca.

Arsenal get patient … and get their reward. Some metronomic passing, then suddenly a shift through the gears, as White and Tzolis combine crisply down the inside-right, cutting back for Odegaard, who pearls a rising shot across Milinković-Savić, off the left-hand post and in! What a strike!
73 min: Gyökeres and Saka, who have both been ineffective this evening, make way for Madueke and Havertz.
72 min: This game has become scrappy, and it’s probably doing Napoli more of a favour.

70 min: Tzolis meets a ball dropping towards the Napoli penalty spot … and nearly launches his shot into orbit. In terms of slapstick and comedic timing, it was almost perfect. In footballing terms, not so much.
68 min: The pace drops. It is warm in Naples after all, 27 degrees centigrade at kick-off according to Uefa’s official thermometer.
66 min: A double change for Arsenal as Merino and Eze make way for Guimarães and Tzolis.

65 min: De Bruyne, under no pressure, butchers a simple pass meant for Lobotka, in acres on the right flank. The crowd groan as the ball sails into the stand. The veteran midfielder has had a bit of a shocker so far.
63 min: Rice makes himself a little bit of time and space to the right of the Napoli D, then lashes a wild shot high and well wide right.

62 min: Hojlund strides down the left but can’t get past Gabriel as he reaches the edge of the box. His shot is deflected, and De Bryune chases after the loose ball, but he doesn’t have the legs to get past Hincapie.
61 min: Vergara also wastes little time in getting involved … but upon tearing down the left, he ruins it all by yanking a dismal cross straight into the arms of Raya.

60 min: The newly arrived Favasuli comes sliding in on Merino at 101 miles per hour. He times his tackle perfectly – just – and the crowd enjoyed that very much. A nanosecond one way or the other, though, and the Napoli sub would have been in a world of bother. He was fully committed, put it that way.

58 min: Santos left White in the dust there, such a cheeky and skilful run, but looks to have injured himself in the process. He departs, along with Politano, the pair replaced by Favasuli and Vergara.

56 min: Santos knocks the ball past White down the left and rounds the defender, then tears away. Lovely play. He shuttles the ball infield for De Bruyne, who looks for Hojlund but his radar is wonky. That’s not his first misplaced pass of the evening, and the home crowd aren’t 100 percent happy with him.
55 min: Rice clumsily clanks into Santos, and pressure that had been building for several minutes is suddenly released. Napoli so grateful for the breather.
53 min: Arsenal are pushing Napoli back. The hosts can’t get out. There’s no option for them other than long to Hojlund. The nearly-all-reds well on top.
52 min: Odegaard, dictating the tempo now from a deep position, loops another pass into the Napoli box. Again for White, but this time down the left, and not so elegant as before. Goal kick.

50 min: Odegaard suddenly springs into action, elegantly wedging a pass down the inside-right channel and into the box for White, who heads across the face of goal. Hincapie should ram home from close range, but somehow manages to leather the ball over the bar. Not for the first time tonight we say: Arsenal should be leading.
49 min: To a chorus of impatient whistling, Arsenal stroke the ball around, this way and that, 30 yards from the Napoli goal. There’s no way through the defence.

47 min: Milinković-Savić has got the mother of all hipster’s beards. He looks like he should be behind the counter at a record store, or running a micro-brewery. While he finds his feet at one end of the park, Napoli make good down the other, and Gilmour takes a whack from distance. Easy for Raya.

Napoli get the second half started. Milinković-Savić has replaced Meret in their goal. “As Big Ron used to say, ‘If you look good, you play good’,” begins Alan Baverstock. “Well, Arsenal are looking crap in all red with white sleeves once again, as anyone would, so don’t expect too much. So close, yet so far from Bill Shankly’s switch to all red at Liverpool: ‘The players looked like giants,’ he said, ‘And we played like giants.’”
Half-time fag break postbag ... which for some reason is tobacco-infused.

“Well, sir, can they boogie without the Great Scott? Presumably Mr McT is in the stand somewhere, a crafty fag on the go, cupped between thumb and index finger and held behind the back, just in case the cameras spot him” – Justin Kavanagh
“Just checking: Gyökeres is still there, right? He hasn’t gone for a lie down or some mid-half snus?” – Adam Walker

“I understand that winning games builds psychological momentum, but I feel that Arteta could use some of these essentially meaningless league phase matches to give his most overworked players the night off. Does Rice need to be on the field? Yeah, if you want to maximise your chances of winning this game. But given how exhausted he looked at the end of last season, it might be good to rest him” – Kári Tulinius

“Can you put that photo of Kai Havertz back up? At least then Arsenal fans will have a useful striker to look at. And it’d be no more immoble than the one on the pitch” – Charles Anaki [Click here to relive some of that Hot Havertz Action]
Half-time ad break. Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!
It’s been good, but not great.

45 min +2: Saka goes long. There’s a bit of pinball, before Hincapie tries to catch Meret out with a cheeky threaded shot towards the bottom left. There’s no pace on the shot, and it’s easy for the keeper.
45 min +1: The first of two additional minutes, and Konsa’s sheer determination down the right wins Arsenal a corner. Just enough time to take it!

45 min: Arsenal should be leading. Odegaard slides a pass down the inside-right channel to release Saka into the Napoli box. Saka is one on one with Meret, and looks for the top left, but gets it all wrong, the ball sailing miles off target to the left. The offside flag pops up to momentarily save Saka’s blushes … but replays show he was comfortably onside. That’s a huge opportunity passed up.

43 min: The free kick, then. A big faff, and a big waste. But Arsenal come again, Odegaard curling in from the left. Meret, who looks fit and healthy to the naked and untrained eye, punches clear acrobatically.

42 min: This game has slipped into Basketball Mode. Saka with a dribble down the right. His cutback for Rice is intercepted. Olivera probes down the left but can’t get past Konsa. Eze scampers up the other end, and is skittled by Gilmour, who goes into the book. A free kick 30 yards out, just to the left of centre.

40 min: Olivera swats Saka off the ball and sends Santos off on a wild run down the left. Santos nearly gets the better of Konsa … but the Arsenal defender somehow sticks to his side like glue, and eventually does some swatting of his own. Santos goes over, and wants a free kick, but he’s not getting one.
39 min: Politano’s in-swinging shot from the right flies straight at Raya. Arsenal counter, and Saka hoicks a dreadful effort miles over the bar.
38 min: … though having said that, Napoli’s back-up keeper Milinković-Savić is furiously prepping in the dugout. Meret puts his boot through a clearance, meanwhile, so perhaps all’s well. Let’s see.
37 min: Meret is fine to continue, and restarts the game. Everyone refreshed.
36 min: The game doesn’t restart immediately, because Meret has a problem. On come the physio. Everyone else takes the opportunity to snorkel some isotonic treats.
35 min: Rice buys a ticket from 25 yards. High and wide.

bodyEn: After their record-breaking feats last year in the Champions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.

Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 that Arsenal were not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances.
Yet they were deserved winners in the end and the substitute Noni Madueke should have made the ­victory more comprehensive late on.

Having come so close to breaking their duck in this competition last year after becoming the first team to win all eight of their league stage matches, Arsenal look capable of going one better this time if Ødegaard can keep up this sparkling form.

He now has four goals in his last five games after scoring once in all competitions last year and it was the Norway captain whose name was being chanted by the fans who were kept behind more than an hour after the final whistle.

“That’s what we need – players with that mindset to decide the game and to play with that personality,” said Arteta. “He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games and I feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in. He’s got that edge and he’s now got different relationships around him [in the team] as well. That helps.”

Arteta has bad memories of this stadium after being sent off in a 2-0 defeat during the Champions League group stage in 2013. But Arsenal’s most recent match here ended in victory as they qualified for the Europa League semi-finals under Unai Emery in 2019. Both clubs have been crowned domestic champions since then, with Napoli ending their 33-year wait in 2023 then doing it again two years later. Yet Champions League success has continued to elude them after finishing 30th in the league phase last season.

That was in stark contrast to Arsenal, who were unbeaten over 14 matches before falling at the final hurdle. It was telling that Arteta kept faith with four of his back five that started against Chelsea on Sunday, with Piero Hincapié replacing Riccardo Calafiori at left-back but failing to match the Italian’s finishing ability with one glaring miss. Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyökeres also made their first starts of the season but largely disappointed, with the Sweden striker making way for Kai Havertz just before Ødegaard’s winner.

Those Arsenal supporters that did make it to southern Italy had no problem making themselves heard throughout, with plenty of empty seats in the home sections despite Max Allegri’s attempts to rally Napoli’s fans beforehand. The game quickly settled into a pattern as the visitors set up camp in Napoli’s half and the hosts attempted to hit them on the break. Kevin De Bruyne – no stranger to facing Arsenal after a decade in the sky blue of Manchester City – forced David Raya into a rare mistake after a typically driving run through the midfield but the ball was scrambled away to safety.

That came just after a spectacular overhead kick from Bukayo Saka at the other end had been saved by Alex Meret. Merino should have scored when he was set up by Eze’s clever header across the face of goal before Ben White drilled a shot straight into Meret’s grateful gloves.

Matteo Politano managed to test Raya again as Napoli continued to find gaps in Arsenal’s normally watertight defence. Saka blazed over after a brilliant through ball from Ødegaard on the stroke of half-time, with replays confirming the assistant had been wrong to raise his flag.

Meret did not return for the second half and was replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, once on Manchester United’s books. The Serbia goalkeeper was a mere spectator for a flowing Arsenal move featuring a sumptuous scooped pass into the area that ended with Hincapié missing the target after being picked out at the far post by Ben White’s header. Suddenly Napoli found themselves suffocated by a blanket of red. Allegri, who knows what it feels like to have lost in a Champions League final after suffering that fate twice in three years at Juventus, responded by switching to a back five and trying to hang on.

Arsenal’s pressure eventually told when another substitute, Christos Tzolis, exchanged passes with White and teed up Ødegaard, whose shot flew in off the post despite Milinkovic-Savic just getting his fingertips to the ball. Havertz had a goal disallowed for offside in injury time, but the mission was already complete.
